title: Of smells
paragraphs: It has been said of some — as of Alexander the Great — that their sweat gave off a fragrant smell, the result of some rare and extraordinary constitution into the cause of which Plutarch and others have inquired. But the ordinary constitution of human bodies is quite otherwise, and their best and chief excellence is to be free of any smell at all. Even the sweetness of the purest breath has nothing more perfect about it than to be without any offensive smell, like the breath of healthy children — which is what made Plautus say of a woman:
"Mulier tum bene olet, ubi nihil olet."
["She smells sweetest who does not smell at all." — Plautus, Mostellaria, i. 3, 116.]
And those who go in for fine exotic perfumes are with good reason to be suspected of some natural defect they are trying to cover up with these scents. To smell, even sweetly, is to stink:
"Rides nos, Coracine, nil olentes Malo, quam bene olere, nil olere."
["You laugh at us, Coracinus, because we have no scent; I would rather, than smell well, not smell at all." — Martial, vi. 55, 4.]
"Posthume, non bene olet, qui bene semper olet."
["Posthumus, the man who always smells well does not smell well." — Idem, ii. 12, 14.]
I am, even so, a great lover of good smells, and equally a hater of bad ones, which I also catch from a greater distance, I think, than other men:
"Namque sagacius unus odoror, Polypus, an gravis hirsutis cubet hircus in aliis Quam canis acer, ubi latest sus."
["My nose is quicker to scent a foul sore or a rank armpit than a sharp dog is to smell out a hidden sow." — Horace, Epod., xii. 4.]

Of smells, the simple and natural ones seem to me the most pleasing. Let the ladies look to it, for it is mostly their concern. In the deepest barbarism, the Scythian women, after bathing, used to powder and crust their faces and their whole bodies with a certain fragrant drug that grew in their country, and when this was cleaned off and they came to be with their men, they were found perfumed and silky. It is hard to believe how strangely all sorts of odours cling to me, and how readily my skin takes them up. The man who complained that nature had not given mankind a vehicle to carry smells to the nose had no reason for it — they do that on their own, especially in my case. My moustache, which is thick, does the office for me: if I stroke it with my gloves or handkerchief, the smell will not leave it the whole day; it tells where I have been. And the close, sweet, devouring, viscid, melting kisses of youthful ardour in my wanton age left a sweetness on my lips for hours afterwards. And yet I have always found myself little subject to the epidemic diseases that are caught either by contact with the sick or bred by the contagion of the air, and have escaped those of my time, several sorts of which have visited our cities and our armies. We read of Socrates that though he never left Athens during the frequent plagues that ravaged the city, he alone was never infected.

Physicians could, I believe, draw more use out of odours than they do, for I have often noticed that they cause an alteration in me and work on my spirits according to their several qualities; which leads me to approve of what is said — that the use of incense and perfumes in churches, so ancient and so universally taken up in all nations and religions, was intended to cheer us, to rouse and purify the senses, and so the better to fit us for contemplation.

I would have liked, the better to judge of it, to have tasted the culinary art of those cooks who had so rare a way of seasoning exotic odours with the relish of meats — as was particularly noted in the service of the king of Tunis, who in our day landed at Naples for an interview with the Emperor Charles. His dishes were larded with fragrant drugs to such an expense that the dressing of one peacock and two pheasants amounted to a hundred ducats; and when the carver came to cut them up, not only the dining room but every apartment of the palace and the streets nearby were filled with an aromatic vapour that did not soon disperse.

My chief concern in choosing lodgings is always to avoid a thick and stinking air; and those beautiful cities, Venice and Paris, lose much of my fondness for them — the one through the offensive smell of her marshes, the other through her dirt.
